summary: EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) lets a peer re-authenticate quickly through any authenticator, while Authenticated Anticipatory Keying (AAK) sets up cryptographic keys ahead of a move. This RFC defines extensions so ERP can support AAK.

eli5.summary: When you walk from one Wi-Fi spot to another, getting keys early makes the switch quick. This lets the system prepare keys before you arrive.

questions: how to speed up eap handover with anticipatory keying
what is anticipatory keying in eap
what is a candidate attachment point
what is the e flag in eap initiate re-auth
subtitle: How a device can get Wi-Fi or mobile keys prepared at the next access point before it arrives there.

tldr.problem: When a device moves between network attachment points, repeating a full EAP authentication at the new one is slow. Anticipatory keying prepares keys on a candidate access point ahead of the move, but ERP had no way to carry that request.
tldr.mechanism: ERP/AAK reuses the ERP packets and adds an E flag for early authentication, plus new fields such as CAP-Identifier. The server derives a pre-established master session key (pMSK) for the named candidate and sends it to that candidate over AAA.
tldr.outcome: A peer can have keying material waiting on a Candidate Attachment Point before handover. RFC 6630 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 6630 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text builds on RFC 5296 (ERP) and RFC 5836 (the early authentication problem statement).

sections.title: Why Early Keys Help
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a generic framework for many authentication methods. When a device moves to a new authenticator, it is desirable not to repeat the whole EAP exchange. The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP, defined in RFC 5296) gives a quick, method-independent way to re-authenticate with an EAP re-authentication server through any authenticator.

Authenticated Anticipatory Keying (AAK, from RFC 5836) goes one step further. It establishes keying material on one or more Candidate Attachment Points (CAPs) before the handover, and it uses the AAA infrastructure to transport the keys. RFC 6630 defines the extensions that let ERP carry AAK.
sections.eli5: Imagine you know you will soon walk into the next classroom. If the teacher there already has your name tag ready, you do not have to wait in line. This document lets the network hand over that name tag early.

sections.title: The ERP/AAK Exchange
sections.content:
ERP/AAK lets the peer ask for keying material to be set up on a single CAP before the peer reaches the candidate access network. The document assumes that the peer supports ERP/AAK, that it has already completed a full EAP authentication, and that either the peer or its Serving Attachment Point (SAP) knows the identities of neighboring attachment points.

The peer can start the exchange on its own, or in response to an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message from the SAP. In the second case the SAP MAY include the identity of a CAP it is adjacent to. The peer SHOULD override it with its own choice if it knows which CAP it will move to.

The peer then sends EAP-Initiate/Re-auth with the E flag set. It carries the keyName-NAI, the CAP-Identifier, the integrity key (rIK) based protection and a sequence number for replay protection. The realm in the keyName-NAI is used to locate the peer's ERP/AAK server. The SAP SHOULD verify the message. If that fails, the SAP MUST send an EAP-Finish/Re-auth with the Result flag set to '1' (Failure). Otherwise it wraps the message in AAA and forwards it to the server.

The server MUST check the rIK, the freshness of the message and the peer's identity, and then authorize the CAP. If all goes well it MUST derive a pMSK for that CAP and transport it to the CAP over AAA. It SHOULD then answer with an EAP-Finish/Re-auth with the E flag set, naming the authorized CAP and the pMSK lifetime, via the SAP.
sections.eli5: You tell your current helper which room you are heading to. The helper asks the office, the office checks who you are and sends a secret key to that room, then tells you it is done.

sections.title: The ERP/AAK Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
The key hierarchy is similar to ERP's. The pre-established Root Key (pRK) is derived from the EMSK if the peer is in its home AAA realm, or from the DSRK if the peer is in a visited realm. If the peer was already authenticated by ERP or ERP/AAK, the DSRK SHOULD be reused directly. The pre-established Master Session Key (pMSK) is derived from the pRK, and it is established for a CAP when the peer early authenticates.

Both derivations use the KDF from RFC 5295. The pRK is KDF (K, S) with K being the EMSK or DSRK and S being the pRK label, a zero byte and a length. The label is the IANA-assigned string EAP Early-Authentication Root Key@ietf.org. The pMSK is KDF (K, S) with K being the pRK and S being the pMSK label, a zero byte, the sequence number (SEQ) and a length. Its label is EAP Early-Authentication Master Session Key@ietf.org.

SEQ is a 16-bit number sent by the peer or the server in the ERP/AAK message. Because it is an input to the derivation, a different sequence number for each CAP gives each CAP its own unique pMSK.
sections.eli5: There is one master key, and from it you make a fresh little key for each new room. Because each little key uses a different number, losing one does not open the others.

sections.title: Packets, Flags and TLVs
sections.content:
ERP/AAK reuses the ERP packet formats and adds a flag, E, to tell early authentication apart from ordinary re-authentication. In EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start the E flag MUST be '1' if early authentication is in use and '0' otherwise. The SAP can add one CAP-Identifier TLV there if it has performed CAP discovery.

In EAP-Initiate/Re-auth the flags are R, x, L and E, followed by a 16-bit SEQ. The L flag requests key lifetimes. The TLVs include keyName-NAI (Type 1, at most 253 octets, exactly one required) and CAP-Identifier (Type 11, a Fully Qualified Domain Name of the CAP, encoded as in RFC 3315). The packet ends with a Cryptosuite byte and an Authentication Tag computed with the rIK. HMAC-SHA256-128 (value 2) is REQUIRED to implement and SHOULD be enabled by default, and HMAC-SHA256-256 is value 3.

In EAP-Finish/Re-auth the R flag is the Result flag ('1' for success). The message holds exactly one keyName-NAI and one ERP/AAK-Key TLV (Type 8). That container carries CAP-Identifier, pMSK Lifetime (Type 10), pRK Lifetime (Type 9) and a list of Cryptosuites (Type 5). The two lifetimes are unsigned 32-bit values in seconds, and they MUST be present if the L flag is set. A peer that receives a message that fails verification, or that has no Authentication Tag, SHOULD discard it silently.

The peer MUST keep retransmission timers for the EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message. If the server never responds after the necessary retransmissions, the peer MUST assume ERP/AAK is not supported by the SAP.
sections.eli5: The messages look like the old ones, but there is one extra tick box that says 'this is the early version'. A secret signature on each message shows it is real.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC checks the design against the AAA key management requirements of RFC 4962, one by one. Its main points are these.

  • Fresh, unique keys: a pMSK is derived on demand when the peer needs a key for a new CAP, so compromise of one pMSK does not compromise another.
  • Limited scope: the pRK derives the pMSK for the CAP, and different sequence numbers for each CAP MUST be used.
  • Replay protection: the peer increments the sequence number by one after sending an ERP/AAK message. The server expects the received number plus one after validating a message.
  • Authentication: ERP provides mutual authentication of the peer and the server, and the CAP is authenticated and trusted by the SAP.
  • Key lifetime: all derived keys are limited in lifetime by that of the parent key or by server policy.
sections.eli5: Every room gets its own key, every message has a counter so old ones cannot be replayed, and the keys stop working after a while.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned five attributes in the EAP Initiate and Finish Attributes registry: Sequence number (Type 7), ERP/AAK-Key (Type 8), pRK Lifetime (Type 9), pMSK Lifetime (Type 10) and CAP-Identifier (Type 11). It also added the two key labels to the USRK Key Labels sub-registry, and reuses the ERP cryptosuites.

New flag registries were created for the three message types. The E flag is 0x80 in EAP Initiate/Re-auth-Start flags and 0x10 in both the EAP Initiate/Re-auth and EAP Finish/Re-auth flags. The other bits are reserved, and new values can be assigned by Standards Action or IESG Approval.
sections.eli5: The authors asked the official list keeper to reserve the new numbers and the new tick box so nobody else uses them.

messages.note: Names the CAP and carries the sequence number.

messages.note: Key distribution to the authorized CAP.

root.label: EMSK or DSRK
root.note: EMSK at home; DSRK in a visited realm

items.label: keyName-NAI
items.desc: Identifies the peer's key and realm; at most 253 octets.

items.label: Cryptosuites
items.desc: List of allowed cryptosuites, one octet each (from RFC 5296).

items.label: Sequence number
items.desc: 16-bit value used to derive the pMSK.

items.desc: FQDN of the candidate attachment point.
